plan.contextChunk: This figure is a potential energy curve for a pair of hydrogen atoms, drawn on a pale blue field with small green spheres added to show the atomic arrangement at three points along it. A tall gradient arrow at the far left, shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, gives the sense of the vertical scale, while the plot's own vertical axis is marked only with a plus sign, a 0, and a minus sign, with a horizontal dashed line drawn across at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Internuclear distance and ends in a magenta arrow pointing right. One magenta curve drops steeply from the upper left, crosses below zero, reaches a rounded minimum, then rises gradually and levels off toward the zero line at large separation. At the top of the steep branch two green spheres overlap, annotated HH (too close). At the right, two widely separated spheres sit above a magenta dashed line joining the letters H and H, annotated H - - - H (too far). At the bottom of the well two just-touching spheres are labeled H-H, and a short vertical dashed line drops from the minimum to the axis, tagged 74 pm, with a green arrow labeled Bond length pointing to it. The depth and position of the single minimum, read against the two extremes flanking it, mark the separation at which attraction and nuclear repulsion balance and fix the length of a covalent bond.

elements: Pale blue plot field with thin dark border
Vertical energy axis marked only with '+', '0', and '–' (no numeric scale)
Horizontal dashed black zero-energy line across the full plot width
Horizontal axis label 'Internuclear distance' below the plot, ending in a magenta right-pointing arrow
Tall gradient arrow at far left, cream at bottom to orange at top, with rotated label 'Energy'
Magenta potential-energy curve: steep repulsive wall at left descending from top, crossing zero, rounded minimum, gradual rise asymptotically approaching zero at right
Two overlapping dark-green spheres at top of the repulsive branch, cyan label 'HH (too close)'
Two just-touching dark-green spheres in the energy well, black label 'H—H'
Two widely separated dark-green spheres at upper right, magenta dashed line joining letters 'H' and 'H' with magenta label 'H - - - H (too far)'
Short vertical dashed line from the curve minimum down to the horizontal axis
Green label '74 pm' beneath the dashed drop line
Green arrow pointing at the minimum with green label 'Bond length'
Movable marker dot on the curve driven by the distance slider
Paired atom sketch that tracks the marker, with attraction/repulsion arrow cues appearing when a region is selected

interactions.teaches: Energy is a single-valued function of separation: pushing the atoms inside 74 pm makes energy climb steeply, pulling them apart lets it relax back toward zero, and only one separation sits at the bottom of the well.
interactions.label: Internuclear distance (pm)

interactions.teaches: Each part of the curve corresponds to a physical situation — repulsion-dominated overlap, balanced bonding, or two essentially independent atoms — so the curve's shape is an energy story, not just a line.

demo_steps.title: Two free atoms
demo_steps.narration: Start with the hydrogen atoms far apart. The marker sits on the flat tail of the curve, essentially at zero energy — the atoms barely feel each other.

demo_steps.title: Attraction pulls them in
demo_steps.narration: As the atoms approach, each nucleus begins to attract the other's electron and the energy falls below zero. The system is becoming more stable than two separate atoms.

demo_steps.title: The energy minimum: bond length
demo_steps.narration: At 74 pm the curve bottoms out. Attraction and nucleus–nucleus repulsion exactly balance here, and this lowest-energy separation is the H—H bond length.

demo_steps.title: Too close: repulsion wins
demo_steps.narration: Squeeze the nuclei closer than 74 pm and the energy rockets up the steep wall. Positive nuclei now repel each other far more than the shared electrons can compensate.

demo_steps.title: Reading the whole curve
demo_steps.narration: Click the repulsive wall, the well, and the far tail in turn: the matching atom sketch lights up, showing why the bond has one preferred length instead of collapsing or flying apart.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A covalent bond has a definite length because energy rises in both directions from the minimum — closer costs repulsion, farther costs lost attraction — so 74 pm is the one separation where the two effects balance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Layout: a tall cream-to-orange gradient arrow labeled 'Energy' stands outside the plot on the far left; the plot itself is a pale blue rectangle with a thin dark border. Y-axis ticks are only '+', '0', '–'; a black dashed horizontal line marks zero about 40% down from the top. The magenta curve enters at the top-left corner, plunges almost vertically, crosses zero roughly a quarter of the way across, reaches a rounded minimum near the lower-left third, then rises smoothly and flattens toward (but just below) the zero line at the right edge. Atoms are small dark-green filled circles with a lighter highlight: an overlapping pair at the very top of the steep branch with cyan text 'HH (too close)'; a just-touching pair inside the well with black text 'H—H' below it; two well-separated circles near the upper right with a magenta dashed connector between letters H and H and magenta text 'H - - - H (too far)'. A thin vertical dashed line drops from the minimum to the axis, tagged '74 pm' in green, with a green arrow and green label 'Bond length' pointing at it from the right. Below the plot, black text 'Internuclear distance' followed by a magenta arrow. Interactive marker: a filled magenta dot that slides along the curve with the distance slider, with the paired-atom sketch redrawn at matching separation directly above it. Clicking a region tints that curve segment and outlines the corresponding atom sketch, showing small red repulsion arrows (pointing apart) on the wall and blue attraction arrows (pointing together) in the well.

authoredContext:
How close are the two nuclei in the H2 molecule? If they are too close, they will repel each other because both are positively charged. Yet if they’re too far apart, they won’t be able to share the bonding electrons. Thus, there is an optimum distance between nuclei that leads to maximum stability (the figure). Called the bond length, this distance is 74 pm in the H–H molecule. Every covalent bond has both a characteristic bond strength and bond length.

A plot of energy versus internuclear distance for two hydrogen atoms. The distance between nuclei at the minimum energy point is the bond length.

A graph of energy versus internuclear distance. A horizontal line separates the positive and negative energy and a curve with a single trough at 74 ppm is shown.

evaluation.notes: A near drop-in static replica of the H2 potential-energy figure (correct Morse-like curve, cyan/magenta/green labels, atom pairs, dashed zero line, gradient energy arrow) with a rich, genuinely pedagogical interaction set (distance slider, 5-step narrated player, clickable/toggleable regions with repulsion/attraction arrows and popups); only small styling differences (thin energy arrow, tail touching the zero line, slightly off-centre x-axis caption) hold it back.
